> Thanks Terry. Your model specification seems to be what I was looking for, but when I fit it using sem(), the F1=~x1 and F2=~x4 coefficients are constrained to be 1, which seems like too many constraints. I assume that lavaan() could be used to fit the model without these extra constraints, but is there a way to do it with sem()?
>

Good point, and no, you can't simultaneously remove the marker-variable constraint and the standardized-latent-variable constraints in the cfa or sem functions.  You can control it in lavaan, though, by setting both "auto.fix.first" and "std.lv <http://std.lv>" to FALSE (actually, those are the default settings in the lavaan function).  You just need to make sure your constructs are adequately identified manually in the model syntax.  Also, you need to either identify ALL parameters in the syntax, or you need to set some lavaan arguments to TRUE, such as automatically estimating the residual variances or intercepts of indicators.  Check whether this model syntax works with the following call to lavaan (notice that the raw and standardized estimates of the regression AND the residual variance are equal):

syntax <- "
F1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
F2 =~ x4 + x5 + x6
F2 ~ Beta*F1
F1 ~~ 1*F1
F2 ~~ ResVar*F2

## MODEL CONSTRAINTS:
ResVar == 1 - Beta^2
"

fit <- lavaan(syntax, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, auto.var = TRUE,
              int.ov.free = TRUE, meanstructure = TRUE)

summary(fit, standardized = TRUE)

                   Estimate  Std.err  Z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
Regressions:
  F2 ~
    F1     (Beta)     0.461    0.064    7.195    0.000    0.461    0.461

Variances:
    F2     (RsVr)     0.788    0.059                      0.788    0.788

Also, if this example is smaller than your full model, then you may need to use more labels/constraints.  For instance, if you have 2 predictors (e.g., F3 ~ F1 + F2), and those predictors are correlated, then you will need to label the residual variance of the outcome, the variances of the predictors (if they are not 1), and the covariance between the predictors, and set the total outcome variance to 1 using all the information about the predictors:

syntax <- "
F1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
F2 =~ x4 + x5 + x6

F3 =~ x7 + x8 + x9
F1 ~~ 1*F1 + Cov*F2
F2 ~~ 1*F2
F3 ~~ ResVar*F3
F3 ~ Beta1*F1 + Beta2*F2

## MODEL CONSTRAINTS:
ResVar == 1 - (Beta1^2 + Beta2^2 + 2*Beta1*Cov*Beta2)
"

Terry

>
> Is there any example on the documentation about how to simulate data in lavaan where a latent interaction (like that f2*f3) is present? if there is not, would you mind sharing one with us, please? it seems like it would be a good thing to have.
>

You could simulate data conforming to the common-factor model "the old-fashioned way," where you generate common and unique factor scores, then combine them using the linear equations that describe your data model.  The steps are essentially:
specify your covariance matrix (and means) among exogenous latent variables
draw a random sample of common factor scores from (1)
specify a regression model for your endogenous latent variables (which can include interactions)
specify a residual covariance matrix for the endogenous latent variables, draw random errors
compute predicted endogenous latent factor scores using (3)
compute latent endogenous factor scores by adding errors from (4) to predicted scores from (5)
specify factor loadings relating the manifest variables to latent factor scores
compute predicted manifest scores using (7)
specify residual covariance matrix for manifest variables, draw errors for each variable
compute manifest variables by adding errors from (9) to predicted scores from (8)
Attached is a script that shows how you would do this for your example.  Since you only had 1 endogenous variable in your example, I skipped the step of specifying the residual covariance matrix of endogenous latent variables, but doing so would entail the same logic described above, and similar to specifying Theta in the attached example.

I've included lots of comments, but let me know if you would like me to clarify anything.

Terry

The paper only discusses factor scores for the continuous case. The
difference between lavaan and LISREL is that LISREL transforms the
factor scores in such a way that their mean vector and covariance matrix
coincides with the model-implied mean and covariances of the latent
variables. In lavaan, we use the more traditional formulas as described
in Lawley & Maxwell (1971). See also Appendix 11 of the Mplus technical
appendices:

http://www.statmodel.com/download/techappen.pdf

For continuous data, nlminb() is not used. We only need to 'optimize' in
the categorical case (again, see Appendix 11 of the Mplus technical
appendices, eq 231: we need to 'minimize' this one).

Hope this helps,

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: estimator - p-value (chi-square)
messages.body_plain:
>
> The p-value is to my understanding not significant. How can I trust the estimated results then?

The null hypothesis for this test is that among the observed variables, the covariances/correlations implied by the model are exactly equal to the covariances/correlations among those variables in the population.  The test is conducted by comparing the observed sample covariances (and means, if those are also included in the model) to the model-implied covariances (and means, if applicable).  The alternative hypothesis is that the model-implied covariances differ from those in the population (as estimated from the sample).  In the example, we fail to reject the null, which means that the model is estimating covariances that are very similar to those in the sample, implying that our model is very similar to the true population model.  So that means we have good reason to trust the results of such a model.

As an aside, the chi-squared statistic is heavily influenced by sample size, so even trivial differences between the true population model and our hypothesized model are likely to be rejected when we have a large sample.  Because our hypothesized model does not need to be exactly correct in order to be useful, many practitioners place less emphasis on the chi-squared test than they do on some alternative indices of fit (although these indices admittedly also have their faults).  For examples of the controversy, you could peruse the articles in the 2007 special issue of the journal Personality and Individual Differences, vol. 42.

> Also, further down, the residuals y4 ~~ y8 are estimated with a p of 0.431 (p.20).
>
>

The test of the correlated residuals y4 ~~ y8 is essentially independent of the test of model fit.  The null hypothesis for parameters' significance tests is the same as it is in linear regression: The slope is zero in the population.  In this case, the null hypothesis is that there is no relationship between errors of measurement for these two variables, and we fail to reject that null, so I suppose you could choose to fix that term to zero, although the fact that the parameter estimate itself is not zero simply implies that you might not have enough power to reject that null at this particular sample size (on the condition that it is not exactly zero in the population).

Terry

The issue is with your higher order factor (IAT). By default latent means in both groups are set to 0 to identify and set the scale of the means. When you use group.equal to equate intercepts, the latent means are fixed to 0 in the first group for scale setting and free to vary in all other groups. With a higher order factor the mean structure must have its scale set in the first and second group. I think if you set the mean of IAT to 0 in your syntax (IAT ~0*1) you should be able to fit the model.

Alex

name (here, the constant '1')

On 11/14/2013 11:38 PM, Alex Schoemann wrote:
> With a multiple group model, inspect(fit, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>") returns a list with
> a covariance matrix for each group.

To replicate the test done by lavaan (ie to test if the covariance
matrices are positive definite), you must compute the eigenvalues:

lapply(inspect(fit, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>"), eigen, only.values=TRUE, symmetric=TRUE)

The eigenvalues should all be strictly positive, although lavaan 0.5-14
has relaxed this a little bit by using a 'tolerance' (ie we allow for
some tiny tiny negative values). After a lot of tinkering, this is what
we now use (assuming the eigenvalues are in eigvals):

any(eigvals < -1 * .Machine$double.eps^(3/4))

if this returns true, you get the warning.

It is also often interesting to look at the correlations (instead of the
covariances):

inspect(fit, "cor.lv <http://cor.lv>")

Yves.

messages.subject: "Factor scores"
messages.body_plain:
I imagine that I am about to come across as one of these cranks who obsesses about just one thing and goes around insisting that everyone agree with him on that one thing.
     Nevertheless . . .
     So many people are posting about the "factor scores" that lavaan, Mplus, and other packages produce.  (LISREL calls them "latent variable scores.")  Please remember that these are not factor scores at all (Guttman 1955).  Common factors are typically indeterminate, which means that they can only be partly reproduced by a weighted sum of observed variables.  This weighted sum part is what software produces when you ask for factor scores, so they would better be called "determinate factor subscores."  These scores do not behave identically with factors.  In particular, they do not conform to the assumed orthogonality between predictor factors and structural error terms.
     The other part of a true factor score is indeterminate.  Any vector which is orthogonal to all the variables in the model and has the same variance as the factor can be used.  This means that a wide variety of such vectors can be constructed.  The different sets if factor scores that thus result need not be highly correlated with each other, and they need not have similar correlations with variables outside the model.  These vectors are arbitrary but not random--they can be highly correlated with outside variables, or they can be orthogonal with such variables.
     A true factor score is a weighted sum of the determinate part and the indeterminate part.  The weighting depends on the degree of indeterminacy in the model.  The more indicators and the stronger the loadings, the less the indeterminacy, but with just a few indicators, as is usually the case in practice, indeterminacy can be fairly high.
     I know, you can't attach a footnote to everything, and we all use shortcuts in describing familiar things.  But I do worry that there are users who are misled by the name "factor score," who believe that the scores produced by software are in some sense perfectly equivalent to the factors in their models.
--Ed Rigdon

To estimate the parameters of the model (in the presence of missing
data), lavaan uses the same optimization algorithm as in the complete
case: quasi-newton (using the nlminb() optimizer). We just use a
different objective function that needs to be minimzed (see
lav_objective.R in the source code).

The EM algorithm is NOT used for estimating the free parameters (in this
case). It is only used to estimate the (sample-based) covariance matrix
and mean vector. This corresponds to the 'unrestricted' model. We only
need this to compute the LRT (the model chi-square test statistic),
since this is just comparing the user-specified (restricted or h0) model
versus the unrestricted (h1) model.

Hope this helps,

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
JB--
     I don't know the context in which Linda was commenting, so it's hard for me to evaluate.  You have to say that these pseudo factor scores are biased because they cannot be consistent.  They cannot be consistent because there is no one true factor score value for these pseudo scores to approach.
     It is hard for me to grasp how it would be different to use them as predictors or as dependents.  If the factor (as is usual) is indeterminate, then the indeterminate piece of the true factor score could be chosen to be equal to the part of any variable not included in the original factor model which is orthogonal to the variables in the original model.  Alternatively, as Louis Guttman showed, you could create another set of factor scores where the indeterminate piece is -1 times that same component.  Or the indeterminate part could be "white noise," but that's not necessary.  All three sets of scores could be equally appropriate sets of factor scores for the same factor.  So different choices for this indeterminate component would have consequences for your results, whether the factor scores are in the role of predictor or dependent.
     Regarding latent growth modeling, the answer depends on whether the same rank problem arises in growth models that arises in conventional factor models.  At root, factor indeterminacy is a rank problem.  In a conventional factor analysis, you have p observed variables, so the rank of the observed covariance matrix is p.  On the other side, you have p specific factors (error terms) plus the common factor, which are all presumed independent of each other.  So when you try to turn the p dimensions of information in the data into p + 1 dimensions of information, you get indeterminacy.
     If you have the same assumption of independence in a latent growth model, then you have the same indeterminacy problem.  In a typical latent growth model, you impose constraints on the error term variances, but I think you are still dealing with p error terms, plus, say, the intercept and slope factors.  So I would expect that you face the same problem.  I would be happy to be proven wrong.
--Ed Rigdon

By using the 'control' argument. You can change all the control
parameters of the nlminb() function using this argument. See ?nlminb for
an overview.

Changing the default maximum number of iterations can be done like this:

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, control=list(iter.max=5))

But the default number is already very high (10000). You may want to
relax the stopping criteria. In particular, the rel.tol and abs.tol
values. The latter is only relevant if you have a saturated model, and
the mimimum of the objective function is zero (as in a regression
model). The default value of rel.tol is 1e-10. To relax this, you can try eg

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939,
control=list(rel.tol=1e-8), verbose=TRUE)

Users of other software can still utilize this function by supplying raw data and model-implied covariance/means instead of a lavaan object, and they can request only the transformed data (to bootstrap themselves) or a list of bootstrap samples, with the option to write either to a file for use in another program.

Hi Roman,

This is a large model, but your sample size is rather small (N=251). If
you consider your observed variables as ordinal, and you have on average
3 indicators per latent variable, you already have 245 free parameters.
Many more if you have more indicators per latent variable.

> I noticed that I get significantly better results when I use the DWLS
> estimator as opposed to the ML or MLM.

Hm. Since you have a 7 point scale, you have either rather extreme
skewed/kurtotic data, or (more likely in this case), the DWLS estimator
fails because there is simply not enough data to get reliable estimates.

> When I fit the model with DWLS however, I get several warnings which I

> Warning messages:
> 1: In lavSampleStatsFromData(Data = lavaanData, missing = lavaanOptions$missing,  :
>    lavaan WARNING: number of observations (251) too small to compute Gamma

Ah. This one is serious: it means that the estimation of 'Gamma' (the
asymptotic variance matrix of the sample statistics, or the inverse of
'W' in DWLS) is most likely unstable, due to the sample size being too
small...

All following warnings are caused by this too.

> Questions:
>
> 1) Is it ok to use the DWLS predictor in my case?

I'm afraid not. I would use MLM or MLR instead.

> 2) Do I have to worry about the warnings?

Yes.

> 3) I have a 1st order (ref2) factor whose predictors have very very low
> estimates. The estimate of this first order factor on the second order
> factors is subsequently extremely high.

It would seem that the indicators of 'ref2' have little in common...
What about a small model with only this factor?

Hope this helps,

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
On 11/22/2013 11:29 PM, Jarrett Byrnes wrote:
> Here's a reproducible example with data.  Note how the R^2 value for y2
> changes.

Thanks. This helps. But I don't think anything is wrong here.

  I think it has something to do with the 0* for the second
> predictor in mod2

You get the same result if you omit the 0*x term. You can already see
the difference if you request the standardized solution:

library(lavaan)
set.seed(2002)
adf <- data.frame(x=rnorm(100), x1 = rnorm(100), y1 = rnorm(100), y2 =
rnorm(100))

mod1 <- ' y2 ~ x + x1 + y1 '

mod2 <- ' y2 ~ x + x1 + y1; y1 ~ x1 '

fit1 <- sem(mod1, adf)
fit2 <- sem(mod2, adf)

summary(fit1, standardized=TRUE)

Variances:
     y2                0.743    0.105                      0.743    0.935

summary(fit2, standardized=TRUE)

Variances:
     y2                0.743    0.105                      0.743    0.923

But in mod1, 'y1' is simply an exogenous variable; while in mod2, 'y1'
is not exogenous anymore, since it is the dependent variable in the
second equation.
In the 'Std.all' column, the regression parameters are standardized
based on the  variances (or residual variances) of the observed
variables; however, this number is not the same for 'y1' in both models.
Hence the difference.

(PS: the resid(fit, "casewise") function has been fixed in 0.5-15 and
should now work correctly with exogenous variables)

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
> I know this: In the lavaan, I have to make new variables for interaction terms in data.frame by myself before execute lavaan.
> But, I want to make a testing interaction hypothesis (or a term) directly. Because, factor structures are 2nd-ordered structure. I don't know how make new interaction terms in data.frame for 2nd-ordered structure.
>

lavaan cannot estimate interactions among latent variables.  The only software that can do so in the way you want, is Mplus, using the "XWITH" operator.  In any other software, your alternatives are to use the product-indicator approach (see the indProd() function in the semTools package to make this task easier) or to extract your factor scores from the hierarchical CFA of your latent variables, then fit a regression model with lm() that can include the interaction term.  I would not recommend the factor scores unless you evaluate them and they have very high correspondence with the latent factors (e.g., high validity measures, almost identical correlation matrices) -- if the factor scores are not well estimated, then any interaction effect would likely be attenuated.

Another option would be to use WinBUGS or OpenBUGS to estimate a Bayesian model, which draws factor scores at every iteration before drawing parameters, so you can get a posterior distribution of the interaction effect as easily as you can for the main effects.  Details are in a recent book that includes syntax examples for all their models:

http://www.wiley.com/WileyCDA/WileyTitle/productCd-0470669527.html

Terry

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm trying to use Lavaan 0.5-15 to estimate a growth model with two groups where most of the variances are free but a few (one in each group) are fixed to 0.

Using the following model as an example (propToll.0, propToll.1., etc. are continuous variables ranging from 0 to 1):

i =~ 1*propToll.0 + 1*propToll.1 + 1*propToll.2 + 1*propToll.3 + 1*propToll.4
s =~ 0*propToll.0 + c(l1_1,l1_2)*propToll.1 + c(l2_1,l2_2)*propToll.2 + start(c(5,5))*propToll.3 + c(l3_1,l3_2)*propToll.3 + 4*propToll.4
propToll.0 ~~ start(c(0,1))*propToll.0 + c(0, v0_2)*propToll.0
propToll.3 ~~ start(c(1,0))*propToll.3 + c(v3_1, 0)*propToll.3
i ~ i*1

When I run this model with the mimic="MPlus" option, the variances of propToll.0 and propToll.3 in both groups are free, but equal and with the same label (v0_2 and v3_1 respectively). If I run it without the mimic="MPlus" option, then the variances of propToll.0 and propToll.3 in both groups are free and not equal but the variances of propToll.0 and propToll.3 are labelled as v0_2 and v3_1 in group 1 and not labelled at all in group 2. I am also able to fix the variances in both groups to different values.

Is there a way for me to fix the variances for only one group to zero while leaving the variance in the other group free?

Thank you for your help.

Richard

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Are there any simple procedures in lavaan that allow us to estimate interactive effects of latent variables? It is possible, of course, to use the Kenny-Judd method to specify the latent product variables "by hand", and to estimate the product indicators and the variances of the latent product variables. However, product variables are generally not normally distributed even if their component variables are normally distributed. I recently read that Klein and colleagues suggested approaches that take into account the degree of non-normality implied by the latent product terms. Klein and Moosbrugger (2000) suggested the "latent moderated structural equations method", which uses a form of the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm. Klein and Muthén (2006) suggested the "quasi-maximum likelihood estimation method", which uses a simpler algorithm but closely approximates results of the former method. Have any of these approaches been incorporated in lavaan?

Is the Lin et al. (2010) approach of orthogonalizing and double-mean-centering the latest state of the art?

Best wishes,

 -- Markus

>

> propToll.0 and propToll.3 in both groups are free, but equal and with

> mimic="MPlus" option, then the variances of propToll.0 and propToll.3 in

> different values.
>

> while leaving the variance in the other group free?

Yes. But you can not mix 'labels' and 'fixed parameter values' in the
same modifier. But you can repeat the same term with different
'modifiers', for example;

propToll.0 ~~ start(c(0,1))*propToll.0 + c(v0_1, v0_2)*propToll.0 + c(0,
NA)*propToll.0

Here we have three times the term 'propToll.0' on the left hand side of
the "~~" operator. The first modifier is for the starting values, the
second for the labels, and the third for fixing/freeing parameters.

Yves.

if (!is.null(baseFit) & is(baseFit, "lavaan")) {

messages.body_plain:
Consider, for example, the following quick and dirty function

r2.lavaan <- function(obj){
  fit <- diag(inspect(obj, "coef")$psi)
  obs <- diag(cov(inspect(fit1, "Data")))

  1-fit/t(obs)

}

This produces the same R2 value for y2 for each model

messages.subject: longitudinal CFA
messages.body_plain:
Dear list members,

I am trying to accomplish a confirmatory factor analysis of a rating scale, assessing measurement invariance across three assessments.

I thought that by using the lavaan.survey package I'd be able to account for dependence among observations. However, thus far I have only managed to produce fit statistics for configural and weak invariance, but not been able to compare these two.

I would appreciate any info on how to get tests of incremental fit.

I'm a rather novice R user (changed from AMOS because of R's versatility) and hope that there is a simple solution.

Regards,

Filip

My model: Three correlated factors with 5, 8, and 7 indicators, respectively. The error variance is set free for two indicators in one factor.
N=1350 with complete data.

#config invariance
mod1fit <- cfa(mod1, dataLong, estimator="MLM", group="time")
survey.design<-svydesign(ids=~id, data=dataLong)
survey.fit<-lavaan.survey(lavaan.fit=mod1fit, survey.design=survey.design)

#weak invariance
mod2fit <- cfa(mod1, dataLong, estimator="MLM", group="time", group.equal="loadings")
survey.fit2<-lavaan.survey(lavaan.fit=mod2fit, survey.design=survey.design)
